header.value: X-Hub-Signature-256 (the older X-Hub-Signature carries a SHA-1 HMAC for compatibility; GitHub recommends the -256 header). Both are sent only when the webhook has a secret configured.
header.quote: X-Hub-Signature is provided for compatibility with existing integrations. We recommend that you use the more secure X-Hub-Signature-256 instead.
header.short: X-Hub-Signature-256 (only when a secret is set)

header_secret_required.value: The signature headers are only sent if a secret is configured.
header_secret_required.quote: X-Hub-Signature-256: This header is sent if the webhook is configured with a secret.

scheme.value: HMAC-SHA256, hex digest, key is the webhook secret.
scheme.quote: This is the HMAC hex digest of the request body, and is generated using the SHA-256 hash function and the secret as the HMAC key.

signed_content.value: The request body (payload contents) exactly as received; the docs say to handle it as UTF-8 and note payloads can contain unicode. The docs do not say how the signed bytes relate to the form parameter when content type is x-www-form-urlencoded: not stated by the provider.
signed_content.quote: The hash signature is generated using your webhook's secret token and the payload contents.

header_format.value: Single value: the literal prefix sha256= followed by the lowercase-looking hex digest (example in the docs: sha256=757107ea...). One signature only; no timestamp element.
header_format.quote: GitHub uses an HMAC hex digest to compute the hash. The hash signature always starts with sha256=.

secret_source.value: You choose the secret yourself when creating the webhook (Secret field); docs advise a random high-entropy string, stored securely and never hardcoded or committed.
secret_source.quote: You should choose a random string of text with high entropy.
secret_source.short: A secret you choose when creating the webhook

secret_storage.value: Keep it out of code and repositories.
secret_storage.quote: Never hardcode a token into an application or push a token to any repository.

secret_scope.value: Set on each webhook's own configuration (repository, organization, or the single webhook of a GitHub App). The docs do not use the phrase 'per webhook' for the secret.
secret_scope.quote: Each GitHub App has one webhook.

timestamp_tolerance.value: not stated by the provider (the signature has no timestamp; replay protection is suggested via X-GitHub-Delivery uniqueness)
timestamp_tolerance.quote: To protect against replay attacks, you can use the X-GitHub-Delivery header to ensure that each delivery is unique per event.

rotation.value: not stated by the provider (no dual-signature or grace-period description found on the pages read)

raw_body_note.value: Verify against the body as received; treat as UTF-8. The page does not use the words 'raw body' in the summary read, only payload contents and UTF-8 handling.
raw_body_note.quote: If your language and server implementation specifies a character encoding, ensure that you handle the payload as UTF-8.

comparison_note.value: Never compare with a plain ==; use a constant-time comparison.

node.value: import { Webhooks } from "@octokit/webhooks"; const webhooks = new Webhooks({ secret }); await webhooks.verify(body, signature)  (signature taken from the x-hub-signature-256 header)

python.value: not stated by the provider as an SDK helper; the docs show a manual example using hmac.new(secret_token.encode('utf-8'), msg=payload_body, digestmod=hashlib.sha256) and hmac.compare_digest

dotnet.value: not stated by the provider (the page shows Ruby, Python, JavaScript and TypeScript examples only)

value.note: Payload is the 13 characters Hello, World! with no newline. Recomputed during research: it matches.

published_test_vector.quote: secret: It's a Secret to Everybody payload: Hello, World! If your implementation is correct, the signatures that you generate should match the following signature values: signature: 757107ea0eb2509fc211221cce984b8a37570b6d7586c22c46f4379c8b043e17 X-Hub-Signature-256: sha256=757107ea0eb2509fc211221cce984b8a37570b6d7586c22c46f4379c8b043e17

method_and_content_type.value: HTTP POST. Content type chosen when the webhook is created: application/json (JSON as the raw body) or application/x-www-form-urlencoded (JSON sent as a form parameter called payload).
method_and_content_type.quote: application/json will deliver the JSON payload directly as the body of the POST request.

content_type_form.value: Form encoding wraps the JSON in a field named payload.
content_type_form.quote: application/x-www-form-urlencoded will send the JSON payload as a form parameter called payload.

user_agent.quote: This header will always have the prefix GitHub-Hookshot/.

event_type_location.value: X-GitHub-Event request header. Many events also have an 'action' field in the body, so check both.
event_type_location.quote: X-GitHub-Event: The name of the event that triggered the delivery.
event_type_location.short: X-GitHub-Event header, plus action in the body

delivery_id.value: X-GitHub-Delivery header (a GUID). A redelivery keeps the same X-GitHub-Delivery as the original.
delivery_id.quote: X-GitHub-Delivery: A globally unique identifier (GUID) to identify the event.

delivery_id_redelivery.quote: If you request a redelivery, the X-GitHub-Delivery header will be the same as in the original delivery.

other_headers.quote: X-GitHub-Hook-ID: The unique identifier of the webhook.

handshake.value: A ping event is sent when a webhook is created (event name ping; body has zen, hook_id and hook). It is a confirmation, not a challenge; no response body is required by the docs. Handle it (or ignore it) and return 2xx.
handshake.quote: The ping event is a confirmation from GitHub that you configured the webhook correctly.
handshake.short: ping event when the webhook is created; answer 2xx

handshake_on_create.quote: After you create a new webhook, GitHub will send you a simple ping event to let you know you've set up the webhook correctly.

handshake_handler_note.quote: as well as the ping event that GitHub sends when you create a webhook.

batching.value: not stated by the provider as a batching rule; each delivery carries one event named by X-GitHub-Event
batching.quote: X-GitHub-Event: The name of the event that triggered the delivery.

payload_size_cap.value: 25 MB; larger events are not delivered at all.
payload_size_cap.quote: Payloads are capped at 25 MB. If an event generates a larger payload, GitHub will not deliver a payload for that webhook event.

success_status.quote: Your server should respond with a 2XX response within 10 seconds of receiving a webhook delivery.

response_deadline.value: 10 seconds; after that GitHub terminates the connection and counts the delivery as failed.
response_deadline.quote: If your server takes longer than that to respond, then GitHub terminates the connection and considers the delivery a failure.

retries.value: No automatic retries: GitHub does not automatically redeliver failed deliveries. You redeliver manually (UI or REST API) for deliveries from the past 3 days.
retries.quote: GitHub does not automatically redeliver failed deliveries.
retries.short: None automatic; redeliver by hand within 3 days

redelivery_window.quote: You can redeliver webhook deliveries that occurred in the past 3 days.

disabling.value: not stated by the provider (no page read says GitHub disables a webhook after failures)

duplicates.value: not stated by the provider as a duplicate-delivery warning. The docs suggest X-GitHub-Delivery to make sure each delivery is unique per event (framed as replay protection), and redeliveries reuse the id.
duplicates.quote: you can use the X-GitHub-Delivery header to ensure that each delivery is unique per event.

async_processing.value: Docs recommend queueing so you can answer quickly.
async_processing.quote: you may want to set up a queue to process webhook payloads asynchronously.

common.meaning: A commit or tag was pushed, or a branch or tag deleted, or a repo created from a template.
common.quote: This event occurs when there is a push to a repository branch.

common.meaning: Any activity on a pull request (opened, closed, synchronize, and so on, via the action field).
common.quote: This event occurs when there is activity on a pull request.

common.meaning: Activity on an issue (opened, closed, labeled and so on).
common.quote: This event occurs when there is activity relating to an issue.

common.meaning: A comment on an issue or pull request was created, edited or deleted.
common.quote: This event occurs when there is activity relating to a comment on an issue or pull request.

common.meaning: Release activity (published, created, edited, and so on).
common.quote: This event occurs when there is activity relating to releases.

common.meaning: A GitHub Actions workflow run changed state (requested, in progress, completed).
common.quote: This event occurs when there is activity relating to a run of a GitHub Actions workflow.
This event occurs when there is activity relating to a check run.

common.meaning: A GitHub App installation was created, deleted, suspended and so on.
common.quote: This event occurs when there is activity relating to a GitHub App installation.

common.meaning: A branch or tag was created.
common.quote: This event occurs when a Git branch or tag is created.

common.meaning: Sent once when a webhook is created, to confirm setup.
common.quote: This event occurs when you create a new webhook.

where_url_is_entered.value: Repository webhook: Settings, Webhooks, Add webhook; set Payload URL, Content type, optional Secret and the events. Organization webhooks need an organization owner. A GitHub App has exactly one webhook, set in its registration.
where_url_is_entered.quote: You must be an organization owner to create webhooks in that organization.

test_tools.value: ping on creation; Recent deliveries list with a Redeliver button (repository admins for repo webhooks, owners for org webhooks); REST API endpoints to redeliver; deliveries from the last 3 days can be redelivered.
test_tools.quote: Only people with admin access to a repository can redeliver webhooks in that repository.

recent_deliveries.value: A recent deliveries log exists for troubleshooting; retention not stated on the pages read.
recent_deliveries.quote: Look at the recent deliveries log for your webhook.

ip_allowlist.value: Published via the GET /meta REST endpoint; changes occasionally, so refresh the allow list periodically.
ip_allowlist.quote: You can use the GET /meta endpoint to find the current list of GitHub's IP addresses.

gotchas.value: 10 second budget; GitHub kills the connection and marks the delivery failed. Queue the work.
gotchas.quote: If your server takes longer than that to respond, then GitHub terminates the connection and considers the delivery a failure.

gotchas.value: Failed deliveries are never retried automatically; if your server is down you must redeliver within 3 days.
gotchas.quote: If your server goes down, you should redeliver missed webhooks once your server is back up.

gotchas.value: Use the SHA-256 header, not the SHA-1 one.
gotchas.quote: We recommend that you use the more secure X-Hub-Signature-256 instead.

gotchas.value: Payloads can contain unicode; handle as UTF-8 when verifying.
gotchas.quote: Webhook payloads can contain unicode characters.

gotchas.value: Oversized events (over 25 MB) are silently not delivered; docs give create with many branches or tags as an example.
gotchas.quote: This may happen, for example, on a create event if many branches or tags are pushed at once.

gotchas.value: Leave SSL verification enabled; docs say use HTTPS.
gotchas.quote: GitHub recommends that you leave SSL verification enabled.

gotchas.value: Check both the event header and the action field before processing.
gotchas.quote: Check the event type and action before processing the event
